healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Argentina. Emergency numbers (107/101/911), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.

recommended: Yellow Fever (recommended for travel to Iguazú Falls area and Northern provinces; required for some national parks)
vaccinations.notes: No required vaccinations for most travelers. Yellow fever vaccination is recommended for travel to northern provinces and Iguazú Falls region. Check specific requirements if visiting national parks in Patagonia. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open 8am-10pm; some 24-hour pharmacies; chains include Farmacity, Dismerca, and regional chains; on-call (de turno) pharmacies listed in newspapers and online
pharmacy.tips: Many common medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful. Bring a list with generic names. Some US OTC medications may not be available — bring your preferred brands. Pharmacias often have a 'pharmacy on call' system for nights/holidays.

water.notes: Tap water is generally safe to drink in Buenos Aires and major cities. In rural areas and smaller towns, bottled water is recommended. In Patagonia (especially rural areas), follow local advisories. Bottled water is widely available everywhere.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Argentina has excellent food safety standards in restaurants and hotels. Asado (Argentine BBQ) is safe at reputable restaurants. Be cautious with street food in informal areas. In Patagonia, stick to well-cooked meats. Empanadas from reputable vendors are generally safe. Dairy products (especially raw cheese) in rural areas should be approached with caution.

travelInsurance.tips: Public hospitals are free but can be slow and bureaucratic. Private healthcare is affordable ($50-150/doctor visit, $300-1,000/day hospital stay) but still requires payment. Travel insurance with medical coverage and evacuation is strongly recommended. Consider coverage for adventure activities (Patagonia trekking, mountaineering) if applicable.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Public hospitals in Buenos Aires and major cities offer good care and are free for tourists, but expect bureaucracy and long wait times. Private clinics are excellent, faster, and affordable by US standards. Many doctors speak English. Pharmacies (farmacias) are widely available.

medications.generalAdvice: Argentina requires all medications to be carried in original packaging with a doctor's note. Antibiotics and many drugs are available OTC with less strict enforcement than in the US or Europe. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a doctor's letter in Spanish or English, and declare them at customs.

controlledSubstances.note: Cannabis is illegal for recreational use in Argentina. Medical cannabis was legalized in 2017 but only for Argentine residents with specific conditions. Do not bring any cannabis or THC products.
Codeine and opioids are controlled substances. Carry original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed for your stay.
Stimulants are controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare to customs. A local prescription may be needed for larger quantities.
Benzodiazepines are controlled and require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity and keep in original packaging.
Regulated due to precursor chemical concerns. Bring phenylephrine-based alternatives instead.

connectivity.simOptions: Claro, Movistar, or Personal prepaid SIMs at airport or city shops. Bring passport. Data is reasonably priced. Cash payments often cheaper than card.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes, restaurants, and hotels in Buenos Aires. Quality good in major cities, limited in rural Patagonia.
connectivity.bestOption: Claro prepaid SIM for best coverage. Buy at Buenos Aires airport. eSIM via Airalo as backup. Note: bring US dollars — better exchange rate on 'blue dollar' market.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants is customary. Round up for taxis. Tip hotel porters AR$500-1000. Propina (tip) jars common at cafes.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in Buenos Aires — Argentines are stylish. Casual elsewhere. No special religious dress codes.
cultural.greetings: One kiss on the right cheek for everyone (men-men, men-women, women-women). Even at first meeting. Handshake only in very formal business.
taboos: Comparing Argentina to other Latin American countries negatively
Rushing meals — dinner starts at 9-10 PM and is a social event
Being punctual to social events (arrive 30-60 min late)
cultural.haggling: Not common at shops or restaurants. Acceptable at artisan markets and when paying cash (ask for 'descuento en efectivo').

safety.lgbtSafety: Argentina is one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries in Latin America. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, and Buenos Aires has a vibrant queer scene. Discrimination protections exist at the national level.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Solo female travel is generally manageable with standard precautions. Buenos Aires and major tourist areas are well-traveled by solo women. Avoid walking alone at night in less-touristed neighborhoods and be cautious with unlicensed taxis.
safety.notes: Argentina is generally safe for tourists who exercise common sense, but petty crime like bag-snatching and pickpocketing is common in Buenos Aires and Rosario. Violent crime exists but rarely targets tourists. The city of Rosario has elevated crime levels due to drug trafficking.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free. UK, EU, Australia, Canada also visa-free. Reciprocity fee eliminated.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: October-April (spring/summer). Patagonia: December-February. Buenos Aires: March-May, September-November (mild). Ski season: June-September.

hospitals.name: Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires
hospitals.notes: One of the best private hospitals in Argentina. English-speaking staff, international patient services.

immediate: Drop, cover, and hold on under sturdy furniture or against interior wall
Stay away from windows and exterior walls
If outdoors, move to open area away from buildings and power lines
after: Check for gas leaks and structural damage before re-entering buildings
Follow INDEC (National Institute of Statistics) and official government alerts
Contact US Embassy if assistance needed: +54-11-5777-4533

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 101)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (101) and ambulance (107) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
